prompt.context: PlastiCo currently sells thin lamination film used to make advertisements and signs (such as ads on the side of city buses, buildings, or billboards). The film is sold in all manner of colors and finishes (matte, gloss, shiny, etc.). PlastiCo currently sells its material in the USA at 10 cents per sq. ft. A European competitor has just finished building a lamination factory in Los Angeles and is approaching PlastiCo's customers, offering to sell product at 9 cents per sq. ft. PlastiCo has hired BCG to help them figure out whether they should match the competitor's price.
prompt.question: Should PlastiCo match the competitor's price of 9 cents per sq. ft.? Evaluate the threat and advise on a pricing strategy.

clarifying_info.q: How is the film transported — can it be shipped by air or sea?
clarifying_info.a: This plastic film is manufactured in giant rolls and cannot be economically transported by air, and cannot survive the harsh conditions of shipment by sea.
The majority of sales are to independent regional suppliers. The remainder is shipped directly to major accounts (major ad companies, Home Depot, etc.).

clarifying_info.q: What is the total market size?
clarifying_info.a: The market is 1 billion sq. ft. per year.

clarifying_info.q: What is PlastiCo's current market share?
clarifying_info.a: PlastiCo currently holds 100% market share — it is a monopoly.

clarifying_info.q: Is the product a commodity or differentiated?
clarifying_info.a: The lamination film is essentially a commodity, meaning customers are sensitive to price and would switch to a cheaper version.

clarifying_info.q: What is the capacity of the new competing plant?
clarifying_info.a: The new competing plant has capacity to produce 250 million sq. ft. per year (25% of the market).

clarifying_info.q: Can the competitor manufacture all of PlastiCo's product range?
clarifying_info.a: 75% of PlastiCo's products can be manufactured by the competitor with no discernible difference. The remaining 25% uses a high-tech coating process that prevents colors from fading and cannot be copied.

exhibits.title: Profit Margins
exhibits.shows: A table showing PlastiCo's profit margin per 1,000 sq. ft. of plastic film, with Revenue, COGS, and Profit line items.

framework: Evaluate two strategic options: match the competitor's price vs. do not match
For each option, analyze: (1) profit impact — revenues and costs; (2) market share implications; (3) long-term strategic consequences
Assess the market: size, current share (monopoly), and how much is threatened by the competitor's capacity
Assess product differentiation: identify what share of volume the competitor can replicate vs. PlastiCo's protected specialty products
Synthesize: compare short-term profit loss of each option and identify break-even market-share loss
Recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: What are PlastiCo's current per-unit economics, and what does profit per sq. ft. equal?
questions.guidance: Use Exhibit 1. Revenue = $100 per 1,000 sq. ft. = $0.10/sq. ft. COGS = $65 per 1,000 sq. ft. = $0.065/sq. ft. Profit = $35 per 1,000 sq. ft. = $0.035/sq. ft. (35% margin).

math.setup: Per 1,000 sq. ft.: Revenue $100, COGS $65, Profit $35. Convert to per sq. ft.
steps: Current price = $0.10/sq. ft., so price cut to $0.09 = $0.01/sq. ft. revenue reduction
math.answer: Current profit = $0.035/sq. ft.; price cut reduces revenue by $0.01/sq. ft.

questions.prompt: If PlastiCo does NOT match the price, what is the expected profit loss?
questions.guidance: The competitor can capture at most its full capacity = 250M sq. ft. (25% of market). Assume 100% conversion of that volume to the competitor. Profit lost = profit margin per sq. ft. times volume lost.

math.setup: Volume at risk = competitor capacity = 250M sq. ft. Profit per sq. ft. = $0.035. Assume 100% of that volume is lost.
math.answer: Profit loss ≈ $8.75M per year if PlastiCo does not match and loses 25% of volume.

questions.prompt: If PlastiCo DOES match the price at 9 cents, what is the expected profit loss?
questions.guidance: Matching price means cutting from $0.10 to $0.09 on ALL 1 billion sq. ft. sold (assuming no market share is lost). Revenue loss = $0.01/sq. ft. × 1B sq. ft.

math.setup: Price reduction = $0.01/sq. ft. on full volume = 1,000M sq. ft. Assumption: no market share is lost.
math.answer: Profit loss = $10M per year if PlastiCo matches price across full volume.

questions.prompt: (Bonus) At what market-share loss would the cost of NOT matching equal the cost of matching?
questions.guidance: Set profit loss from not matching (= $0.035 × 1,000M × x%) equal to $10M and solve for x.

math.answer: PlastiCo would need to lose more than ~28.6% of market share for not matching to cost MORE than matching.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional strategies should PlastiCo consider for the 25% of products that cannot be replicated by the competitor?

categories.name: Pricing the differentiated segment
ideas: Raise prices on the specialty (color-fade-resistant) products since there are no substitutes
Capture maximum producer surplus given inelastic demand for the differentiated 25%
The higher margins on 25% can partially offset revenue lost on the commoditized 75%

categories.name: Defending market share on commodity products
ideas: Match price at $0.09 to retain the 75% of volume at risk
Consider targeted price matching only for at-risk accounts rather than across the board
Lock in major accounts and regional distributors with long-term contracts before competitor gains access

categories.name: Competitive response / long-term moats
ideas: Invest in expanding the high-tech coating (differentiated) product line
Monitor competitor capacity expansion — if they add capacity beyond 250M sq. ft., the situation deteriorates further
Explore cost reduction to restore margins if price is matched
Consider whether the European competitor can eventually solve the transport problem and expand

recommendation: PlastiCo should match the competitor's price of 9 cents per sq. ft. to defend its market position.

Matching costs $10M in annual profit vs. $8.75M if 25% of volume is fully lost — but the do-not-match scenario leaves PlastiCo exposed to further market erosion if the competitor expands capacity beyond 250M sq. ft.
Simultaneously, PlastiCo should maintain (or raise) prices on the 25% of differentiated, color-fade-resistant products where it has no competition, to maximize margins on that protected segment.
risks: Even with a price match, some customers may have already been won over by the competitor, so market share loss is not guaranteed to be zero.
If the competitor later expands capacity, PlastiCo faces additional price pressure with now-reduced margins.
Raising prices on the specialty segment could prompt customers to seek alternatives or reduce usage.
next_steps: Analyze cost structure to identify opportunities to reduce COGS and restore margin at the lower $0.09 price point.
Audit which major accounts and regional distributors are most at risk of switching and prioritize retention outreach.
Assess feasibility of expanding the differentiated (anti-fade) product line to shift a larger share of volume into the protected segment.
Monitor the European competitor's capacity plans and financial health.
